newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile raids German enclave searching for leader.
newsitem.headline: Chile raids German enclave searching for leader.

text.p: Police on motorcycles, trucks and horseback occupied a secretive German colony in Chile on Wednesday seeking to arrest its fugitive leader, Paul Schaefer, who faces charges of sexually abusing children.

More than 200 police pushed into the heavily guarded enclave known as Colonia Dignidad (Dignity Colony) in a convoy of buses, trucks and ambulances following the arrest of two of Schaefer's aides on Tuedsay night.
By nightfall, police were still inside the settlement.
"This is a raid and the objective is the arrest of Paul Schaefer," police spokesman Raul Toro said. He said the raid would last as long as it took to arrest Schaefer.
Wearing bulletproof vests, police met no armed resistance at the electrified, barbed-wire gates to the colony tucked away in the Andean foothills 200 miles (320 km) south of Santiago.
The raid followed a series of brief police inspections that began last month at the colony of traditional Bavarian homes.

The mysterious settlement set up by German immigrants in the early 1960's enjoyed the protection of Chile's past military regime under Gen. Augusto Pinochet, but has come under pressure to reveal its secrets since democracy was restored in 1990.

Schaefer, a corporal in the Nazi army in the Second World War and now in his late 70s, was believed to be holed up somewhere in the property although settlers say they have not seen him for about eight months.
"Schaefer will be detained sooner rather than later," Deputy Interior Minister Belisario Velasco said, adding that officials believed settlers might have unregistered weapons.
Television images showed police with dogs inspecting tunnels and hallways but no obvious signs of resistance.

A brief statement issued by the settlers later said the raid was causing "commotion" among the colony's 300-some residents and warned there would be a "dramatic end" if police did not leave, but gave no specifics.
"The rights of innocent people are being trampled here," said the statement handed to reporters.
Colony members say they fear that Schaefer, charged with molesting at least five Chilean boys at a settlement boarding school, would commit suicide rather than be arrested.

A former Protestant preacher and charismatic speaker, he has been accused of molesting boys at Colonia Dignidad since 1966. Media reports say he fled Germany in about 1957 after charges of fondling youngsters at an orphanage he founded in Bonn.
Colonia Dignidad's leaders also face charges of illegal detention of children, obstruction of justice and tax evasion.

The new child molestation charges, filed last year, have galvanised opposition to the colony in President Eduardo Frei's government and alienated the settlement's one-time supporters among right-wing Chileans.
Members of the past military government often spent their vacations at the scenic settlement. Human rights groups say the Pinochet regime sent political prisoners there to be tortured.
But in 1991, a newly-elected civilian government revoked the colony's status as a charitable organisation.
"We cannot allow...these people to continue living as they have for the past 36 years," Frei said last month.

Defectors from the colony say residents are not allowed to read newspapers or watch television, their mail is censored, youngsters are drugged and subjected to unusual punishments by Schaefer and no dissent to his rule is permitted.
Schaefer is also accused of illegally depriving Chileans of custody of their children.
One woman, Raquel Munoz told the Santiago newspaper La Tercera she sent her 12-year-old son to the colony's hospital for polio treatment 22 years ago, and never saw him again.
"I'm 73 years old now and I'm terrified that God will take me away without ever letting me see my son again," said Munoz.
